title: Why we preregister our EHR analyses
excerpt: Writing the analysis plan before touching outcomes changes which questions we can answer honestly.

content.html:
Electronic health records invite endless re-analysis. Every extraction can be filtered, linked, and re-coded, and each choice moves the estimate a little. We now preregister every EHR analysis before we look at outcome data.

What goes in the plan

  • The target trial: eligibility, treatment strategies, and time zero.

  • The causal diagram and the adjustment set it implies.

  • How we handle missing covariates and loss to follow-up.

What it costs

About two weeks per project. The plan template is on OSF, and the protocol for our registry linkage study is linked from the project page.

A plan written after the results is a description of the results.

title: Notes on multiple imputation with chained equations
excerpt: A working checklist for MICE in R, with the defaults I change and why.

content.html:
These notes collect what I tell students before they run mice() on a real data set.

Set up the predictor matrix first

The default uses every variable to impute every other variable. That is rarely what you want when the data include IDs or derived scores.

library(mice)
imp <- mice(dat, m = 20, maxit = 0)
pred <- imp$predictorMatrix
pred[, "patient_id"] <- 0
fit <- with(mice(dat, m = 20, predictorMatrix = pred), lm(sbp ~ age + bmi))
pool(fit)

Check convergence

Plot the chains with plot(imp). If the means drift after iteration 10, raise maxit and look for variables that predict each other almost perfectly.

content.markdown:
These notes collect what I tell students before they run `mice()` on a real data set.

## Set up the predictor matrix first

The default uses every variable to impute every other variable. That is rarely what you want when the data include IDs or derived scores.

```r
library(mice)
imp <- mice(dat, m = 20, maxit = 0)
pred <- imp$predictorMatrix
pred[, "patient_id"] <- 0
fit <- with(mice(dat, m = 20, predictorMatrix = pred), lm(sbp ~ age + bmi))
pool(fit)
```

### Check convergence

Plot the chains with `plot(imp)`. If the means drift after iteration 10, raise `maxit` and look for variables that predict each other almost perfectly.

title: A short reading list for target trial emulation
excerpt: Five papers I assign before students design their first emulation.

content.html:
Start with these, in this order:

  1. Hernán and Robins on using big data to emulate a target trial.

  2. The protocol checklist papers, for the components of a trial specification.

  3. A worked example with sustained treatment strategies.

  4. A paper on immortal time bias, to see what goes wrong without a clear time zero.

  5. A critique, so the method does not look like a solved problem.

The full citations are on the publications page under the teaching tag.

title: What I learned reviewing 40 survival analyses
excerpt: Most problems came from the time axis, not the model.

content.html:
Last year I reviewed forty manuscripts that used Cox models. The same three problems came up again and again.

  1. Time zero did not match eligibility.

  2. Hazard ratios were reported for crossing curves.

  3. Competing risks were treated as censoring.

The fix for the first one is cheap.
The fix for the third one is not, and it changes the estimand. Reporting a sensitivity analysis is enough. A sensitivity analysis does not fix the estimand.

title: Sharing code with the papers: a checklist
excerpt: What our group checks before a repository goes public with a paper.

content.html:
Every paper from our group ships with code. Before a repository goes public we check five things.

  • It runs from a clean checkout with renv::restore().

  • Paths are relative.

  • Simulated data stand in for restricted data.

  • The README names the R version.

  • A license file exists.

None of this takes long once it is a habit.

title: Hierarchical models for small-area rates
excerpt: Why raw county rates mislead and how partial pooling helps.

content.html:
Raw rates from small counties swing wildly. A county with 40 children and 3 cases has a rate of 75 per 1,000, and nobody believes it.

Partial pooling

A hierarchical model shrinks each county toward the regional mean in proportion to how little data it has. In code the filter is rate < 0.05 & n > 30 for counties we trust without pooling.

model {
  theta ~ normal(mu, tau);
  y ~ binomial_logit(n, theta);
}
